title: Why contact history matters
lines: A robot is preparing fruit. Is its gripper safe to use?
First, the left gripper touches a contaminated tray.
It then carries contamination to the spoon handle.
The robot washes both grippers, but not the spoon. Its handle stays contaminated.
The assistant returns the spoon, contaminating the clean right gripper again.
The fruit-handling plan must change. First, the robot puts down the spoon.
User priorities can favor different treatments. We demonstrate washing with water and wiping with paper.
After treatment, the robot resumes placing fruit.
Planning must decide what to treat, when, and at what resource cost.
The benchmark formalizes this choice as washing or replacing the contact pad. User priorities determine the preferred safe continuation.
HygieneRoboBench tests household planning under contact history, user priorities, and new events.

title: What the benchmark asks
lines: Our 624 instances form 134 task families, covering five activity groups and seven household areas.
Figure three shows three views of these same 624 instances: activity groups, construction designs, and difficulty. The rings partition the same dataset; they are not additional samples.
Each task provides a request, physical observations, history, resources, available events, and ordered user priorities.
Under shared rules, planners return actions, objects, gripper assignments, and schedules, or an infeasible or undetermined judgment.
Controlled pairs change history, priorities, or event information, keeping other task conditions fixed.

title: How tasks and rules are built
lines: Figure two shows how the benchmark is built. Household activities and hygiene guidance feed five shared registries, which define the rules used to construct each task.
Tasks adapt BEHAVIOR-1K activities. Published studies and public-health guidance inform hygiene rules with explicit material and procedure requirements.
In the fruit task, washing requires an empty gripper and treats only its contact pad. The spoon stays separately tracked.
Washing and replacement have abstract time and resource costs, giving planners a common basis for comparison.
For general parameter construction, an LLM screens online time and supply estimates; reviewers check plausibility and relative magnitudes.
Washing saves spare parts. Replacement saves water but produces waste. User priorities determine the preferred safe option.
Two reviewers check applicability, action conditions, and consistency; a third gives final review. Programs separately validate matched conditions and reference targets.

The episode builder combines a base task with histories, priorities, and event information. Matched-condition checks, reference validation, independent replay, and human review govern dataset admission.

title: How submitted plans are evaluated
lines: Independent of the planning solver, the evaluator replays history and checks goals, hygiene, timing, and resource limits.
Holding the spoon violates the washing precondition. Putting it down first satisfies the empty-gripper requirement.
The evaluator recomputes costs and compares them with private reference targets under the same priorities. Planners cannot access these targets.
Safe resolution credits safe completion or correct infeasibility rejection. Optimal safe resolution also requires reference-optimal costs for submitted plans.

title: What the benchmark reveals
lines: We evaluate five language models, Rule-SAT, and Hygiene-NSP on the same 624 instances.
Hygiene-NSP reaches 94.4 percent safe resolution and 90.4 percent optimal safe resolution, the highest overall rates.
DeepSeek produces 98 safe, nonoptimal plans. In 41, water or replacement parts is the first nonoptimal cost dimension.
All seven planners score lower as difficulty increases. Activity breakdowns reveal different strengths: Gemini leads cleaning and laundry.

title: Does changing history change the outcome?
lines: These fruit histories share physical conditions and priorities. Changing whether washing precedes spoon contact changes the contamination state.
Prioritizing spare parts, the contaminated case needs washing before fruit handling. The clean case can continue directly after putting down the spoon.
Swap the histories, keeping saved actions and timing fixed. Direct continuation becomes unsafe. Washing stays safe, but adds unnecessary treatment.
As a control, histories differ on an unused side pad. Neither continuation touches it again. Outcomes stay unchanged.
After relevant-history swaps, none of 1,699 originally safe, optimal replays retain both. All 1,288 irrelevant-history evaluations preserve their outcomes.

title: Priorities and newly revealed events
lines: Priority pairs instead fix history and action costs, testing whether plans adapt when users change their resource preferences.
Hygiene-NSP succeeds on 234 of 268 general pairs and 24 of 25 ranking-flip pairs, leading both groups.
Event tests update history and context. Fifty relevant and fifty irrelevant instances assess safe, optimal continuation after new contact information.
Hygiene-NSP reaches 88 and 92 percent optimal safe resolution. Gemini leads both event conditions.

title: A companion neuro-symbolic planner
lines: Hygiene-NSP grounds requests and priorities with a language model. A trusted compiler checks the structured planning problem.
History replay reconstructs hygiene states. CP-SAT jointly schedules treatment and service actions under user priorities.
Optional state projection retains task-relevant information in a smaller representation, with full-state fallback when needed.
Across 177 paired runs, local planning time improves by a median 20.1 percent across families, excluding language-model calls. Status and cost agree in 175 pairs.

title: Takeaway
lines: HygieneRoboBench connects contact history, resource priorities, and event response: evaluating both safe completion and the right safe choice for the user.
Thank you for watching. Explore the benchmark on the project page.
